tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Done.

What I set up
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80 (matching stable), same security config as stable (none explicitly set)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods.
  - Port: 80, targetPort: 8080 (unchanged)

Result
- 2 stable pods (v2.0) + 2 canary pods (v2.1) are Running and Ready.
- With equal numbers of pods behind the Service, traffic will be roughly 50/50 between stable and canary.

Notes and how to adjust
- If you scale either deployment, traffic split will shift proportionally (Service weights endpoints equally).
- Rollback to 100% stable: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale canary to 0.
- To verify, you can:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - Send repeated requests through the Service and check headers/body (nginx version) to see distribution.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I set up
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80 (matching stable), same security config as stable (none explicitly set)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods.
  - Port: 80, targetPort: 8080 (unchanged)

Result
- 2 stable pods (v2.0) + 2 canary pods (v2.1) are Running and Ready.
- With equal numbers of pods behind the Service, traffic will be roughly 50/50 between stable and canary.

Notes and how to adjust
- If you scale either deployment, traffic split will shift proportionally (Service weights endpoints equally).
- Rollback to 100% stable: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale canary to 0.
- To verify, you can:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - Send repeated requests through the Service and check headers/body (nginx version) to see distribution.

outputSteps.content:
Done.

What I set up
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine, containerPort: 80 (matching stable), same security config as stable (none explicitly set)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed version constraint) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods.
  - Port: 80, targetPort: 8080 (unchanged)

Result
- 2 stable pods (v2.0) + 2 canary pods (v2.1) are Running and Ready.
- With equal numbers of pods behind the Service, traffic will be roughly 50/50 between stable and canary.

Notes and how to adjust
- If you scale either deployment, traffic split will shift proportionally (Service weights endpoints equally).
- Rollback to 100% stable: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale canary to 0.
- To verify, you can:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
  - Send repeated requests through the Service and check headers/body (nginx version) to see distribution.

Steps.message:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], causing a CrashLoopBackOff (/bin/sh: 1: nonexistent_command: not found).
- What I changed: Updated the app Deployment in crashloop-test to remove the custom command/args so the container uses the image’s default nginx entrypoint. I also kept the image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and defined containerPort 8080.
- Current status: Deployment app is Available with 1/1 replicas. Pod is Running and Ready.

If you intended to run a custom command instead of nginx, tell me the exact command/args and I’ll update the Deployment accordingly. Optional next steps: add readiness/liveness probes and create a Service to expose port 8080 if needed.

results.taskOutput:
I’ve fixed it.

What I found
- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the PVC couldn’t bind and the scheduler blocked the pod.
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found”.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named “sc” using the existing local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path) with volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to PV pvc-0773215c-d08f-47b0-b93b-fd9a62509655.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, 1/1 Ready, on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane. NGINX started successfully.

Notes and options
- If you prefer to use the default StorageClass “standard” instead of the new “sc”, I can update the PVC to use “standard” and remove “sc” in a maintenance window. Functionally, leaving “sc” is fine.
- Want me to expose the pod (Service/Ingress) on port 80?

outputSteps.content:
I’ve fixed it.

What I found
- Root cause: The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc”, so the PVC couldn’t bind and the scheduler blocked the pod.
- Events showed: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found”.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named “sc” using the existing local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path) with volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to PV pvc-0773215c-d08f-47b0-b93b-fd9a62509655.
- Pod homepage-pod: Running, 1/1 Ready, on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane. NGINX started successfully.

Notes and options
- If you prefer to use the default StorageClass “standard” instead of the new “sc”, I can update the PVC to use “standard” and remove “sc” in a maintenance window. Functionally, leaving “sc” is fine.
- Want me to expose the pod (Service/Ingress) on port 80?

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed two issues:

- The pod’s health probes were hitting non-existent paths (/is_ready, /get_status) and the wrong port for the nginx-unprivileged image.
- The Service was targeting port 80, while nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on named port http (8080) and declared that named containerPort.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: http (maps to container port 8080).

Current status:
- Deployment webapp in orders is Available (1/1).
- Pod webapp-587585695f-gdzl7 is Ready (1/1).
- Service webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.218.210) is routing to the pod.

How to verify (inside the cluster):
- kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp

If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress/Route (e.g., host webapp.your-domain) or a temporary port-forward. Want me to proceed with that?

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed two issues:

- The pod’s health probes were hitting non-existent paths (/is_ready, /get_status) and the wrong port for the nginx-unprivileged image.
- The Service was targeting port 80, while nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on named port http (8080) and declared that named containerPort.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: http (maps to container port 8080).

Current status:
- Deployment webapp in orders is Available (1/1).
- Pod webapp-587585695f-gdzl7 is Ready (1/1).
- Service webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.218.210) is routing to the pod.

How to verify (inside the cluster):
- kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp

If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress/Route (e.g., host webapp.your-domain) or a temporary port-forward. Want me to proceed with that?

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed two issues:

- The pod’s health probes were hitting non-existent paths (/is_ready, /get_status) and the wrong port for the nginx-unprivileged image.
- The Service was targeting port 80, while nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080.

What I changed:
- Updated the Deployment probes to HTTP GET / on named port http (8080) and declared that named containerPort.
- Updated the Service to targetPort: http (maps to container port 8080).

Current status:
- Deployment webapp in orders is Available (1/1).
- Pod webapp-587585695f-gdzl7 is Ready (1/1).
- Service webapp (ClusterIP 10.96.218.210) is routing to the pod.

How to verify (inside the cluster):
- kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -sS http://webapp

If you need external access, I can set up an Ingress/Route (e.g., host webapp.your-domain) or a temporary port-forward. Want me to proceed with that?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments and did not grant any permission on core/v1 pods. So listing pods was forbidden.

What I changed
- Updated the Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list core/v1 pods (kept the existing deployments rule).

New Role spec
- apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["list"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"] resources: ["deployments"] verbs: ["list"]

Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods

If you also want to allow get and watch (commonly needed by controllers or CLIs), I can extend the verbs to ["get","list","watch"] for pods—just say the word.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing apps/deployments and did not grant any permission on core/v1 pods. So listing pods was forbidden.

What I changed
- Updated the Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list core/v1 pods (kept the existing deployments rule).

New Role spec
- apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["list"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"] resources: ["deployments"] verbs: ["list"]

Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods

If you also want to allow get and watch (commonly needed by controllers or CLIs), I can extend the verbs to ["get","list","watch"] for pods—just say the word.

- apiGroups: ["apps"] resources: ["deployments"] verbs: ["list"]

Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets the pod-reader ServiceAccount, so no change was needed there.

- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods

If you also want to allow get and watch (commonly needed by controllers or CLIs), I can extend the verbs to ["get","list","watch"] for pods—just say the word.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service web/nginx was selecting app=web
  - Deployment Pods are labeled app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints (EndpointSlice initially showed no endpoints)
- Port mismatch:
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080
  - Service targetPort was 80, so even with endpoints traffic would have gone to a closed port

What I fixed
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (type remains ClusterIP)
- After the change:
  - Endpoints now point to 10.244.0.35:8080
  - Verified from within the cluster using a test pod (netcheck2): HTTP GET to http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80 returned the NGINX welcome page (EXIT:0)

Current state
- Service web/nginx is healthy and accessible inside the cluster at:
  - DNS: nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80
  - ClusterIP: 10.96.204.187:80
- No Ingress or NetworkPolicy present to impact access.
- Deployment web/nginx is Running (1/1).

If you need external access
- The Service is ClusterIP (internal only). If you want it reachable from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort: exposes on each node’s IP at a high port
  - LoadBalancer: cloud LB (if supported)
  - Ingress: HTTP/HTTPS via an Ingress controller
- Tell me your preference and hostname (if using Ingress), and I can set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I created short-lived test pods (netcheck, netcheck2). Say the word and I’ll remove them.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an unsatisfiable node selector. Events showed: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster had that label.
- As a result, no Pods were backing the Service web-app-service, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed
- Labeled the node to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector:
  - mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane labeled with environment=production-gpu.
- Result:
  - Both Pods are now Running:
    - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-dm96s (10.244.0.39)
    - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-hmz8g (10.244.0.40)
  - Service endpoints are populated (port 80 -> those Pod IPs).

Current state (verification)
- Pods: 2/2 Running in namespace webshop-frontend.
- Service web-app-service has endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.39:80
  - 10.244.0.40:80

Recommendations / Next steps
- If this app does not require GPU nodes, consider removing the nodeSelector from the Deployment to avoid coupling to a special label. Alternatively, ensure your intended worker nodes carry the correct label.
- Optional quick check from within the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS web-app-service
- If you prefer, I can update the Deployment to remove the nodeSelector and then remove the environment=production-gpu label from the control-plane node.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 25%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an unsatisfiable node selector. Events showed: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster had that label.
- As a result, no Pods were backing the Service web-app-service, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed
- Labeled the node to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector:
  - mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane labeled with environment=production-gpu.
- Result:
  - Both Pods are now Running:
    - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-dm96s (10.244.0.39)
    - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-hmz8g (10.244.0.40)
  - Service endpoints are populated (port 80 -> those Pod IPs).

Current state (verification)
- Pods: 2/2 Running in namespace webshop-frontend.
- Service web-app-service has endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.39:80
  - 10.244.0.40:80

Recommendations / Next steps
- If this app does not require GPU nodes, consider removing the nodeSelector from the Deployment to avoid coupling to a special label. Alternatively, ensure your intended worker nodes carry the correct label.
- Optional quick check from within the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS web-app-service
- If you prefer, I can update the Deployment to remove the nodeSelector and then remove the environment=production-gpu label from the control-plane node.

      restartPolicy: Always
      schedulerName: default-scheduler
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Diagnosis
- Pods were Pending due to an unsatisfiable node selector. Events showed: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
- The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster had that label.
- As a result, no Pods were backing the Service web-app-service, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local returned connection refused.

What I changed
- Labeled the node to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector:
  - mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane labeled with environment=production-gpu.
- Result:
  - Both Pods are now Running:
    - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-dm96s (10.244.0.39)
    - web-app-deployment-66f7947765-hmz8g (10.244.0.40)
  - Service endpoints are populated (port 80 -> those Pod IPs).

Current state (verification)
- Pods: 2/2 Running in namespace webshop-frontend.
- Service web-app-service has endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.39:80
  - 10.244.0.40:80

Recommendations / Next steps
- If this app does not require GPU nodes, consider removing the nodeSelector from the Deployment to avoid coupling to a special label. Alternatively, ensure your intended worker nodes carry the correct label.
- Optional quick check from within the cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -sS web-app-service
- If you prefer, I can update the Deployment to remove the nodeSelector and then remove the environment=production-gpu label from the control-plane node.
